newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh Hill Tracts tense over killings.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh Hill Tracts tense over killings.

text.p: The government on Thursday ordered a probe into the killings of 30 Bengali-speaking settlers by tribal rebels in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts as fears of a backlash gripped the region.
Officials said Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had asked Home (Interior) Minister Rafiqul Islam and four other ministers to fly to the region to find out what had led to the "extreme tragedy".
She had also asked the ministers to "help prevent further barbarity by either the grief-stricken Bengalis or the tribals fearing a backlash", one official told reporters.

The official said many tribespeople opposed the killings and torture by tribal Shanti Bahini (peace force) guerrillas, who seek autonomy for the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts bordering India and Burma.
The guerrillas, most of them Chakma tribesmen, want some 300,000 Bengali settlers expelled from the region, which they consider a tribal homeland.
The rebels abducted 37 settlers on Monday night from a village in the Rangamati district, police said. Army troops recovered 30 bodies, most of them beheaded and bullet riddled, on Wednesday morning.

Two of the abducted settlers managed to flee, although they had been shot and wounded. Five were still missing, police said on Thursday. Troops backed by helicopters were searching for the missing, they said.
"This is the biggest massacre in many years," one defence source told Reuters on Wednesday.
"Most of the bodies have been beheaded and a few bore gunshot marks," one police officer said.
Officials and journalists at Rangamati, 60 km (40 miles) from where the killings occurred, said on Thursday that Bengali settlers, most of them Moslem, were preparing to avenge the deaths.
"They are even preventing post-mortem of the dead," one journalist said.
Schools and markets in Rangamati have remained closed and many residents have fled their homes, he said.
Tuesday's killings occurred despite a ceasefire reached between the rebels and the government two months ago. It is due to expire on September 30.

The Shantis took up arms in 1973 after Bangladesh rejected their demand for autonomy. They opposed the presence of non-tribal settlers, accusing them of grabbing tribal land and threatening tribal culture.
Officials say more than 8,000 rebels, soldiers and civilians had been killed in the insurgency, which has forced thousands of tribal families to flee to northeast India.
